study.title: Psalm 113 The Exalted God who inclines to the humble
study.overview: Psalm 113 calls the people of God to praise the LORD because he is incomparably exalted and at the same time deeply attentive to the needy. The song begins and ends with alleluia, forming a frame of worship. The verses 1-3 call the continual and universal praise to the name of the LORD. The verses 4-6 affirm their greatness above all the nations and the heavens, but also their condescension: he is lowered to observe and act in the human world. The verses 7-9 show this mercy in concrete actions, especially when raising the poor and giving the barren a family and joy.

outline.title: Call to Constant Praise
outline.explanation: The psalm begins with an insistent call for the servants of the LORD to praise him. The name of the LORD represents his person, character and reputation, and must be blessed continually, without limits of time or place.

outline.title: The greatness of the LORD and his attention to the world
outline.explanation: The LORD is above all nations and of all creation, but that time does not make him distant. He leans to see what occurs in the heavens and the earth, showing that his transcendence does not exclude his active care.

outline.title: Mercy that raises the humble
outline.explanation: The psalm describes the LORD as the one who raises the poor from the dust, exalts the needy, and transforms the shame of sterility into family joy. Divine action reaches people without prestige and grants them dignity and future.

study.context: The notes relate this psalm to the so-called great halel, set of psalms used by Jews at solemn festivals, especially at Easter. The notes also note that the Psalms 113 and 114 were recited before the paschal meal, and that the psalm may have been composed after the return of the captivity. This is presented as a possibility in the notes, not as absolute certainty of the text.
study.theology: The psalm unites two attributes that must be held together: the majesty of God and his mercy. He is superior to all nations, but is not indifferent to human suffering. The theology of the text shows that true divine greatness includes graceful closeness to the humble. Praise is born not only from the contemplation of God's power, but also from the recognition that he governs to help the poor, raise the relegated and give life where there was sterility and shame. Thus the psalm presents the LORD as worthy of worship by whom he is and for what he does in the real world.

scholarViews.insight: The name of the LORD reveals his being, character and reputation, and he is exalted in time and space.
The psalm is structured to promote praise to God, calling the people to worship it often and fervently.
The exaltation of the LORD above all nations means that he governs and provides for all, so it must be praised by all.

questions: What changes in our worship when we remember that the Lord is at the same time exalted and close to the humble?
In what practical ways can we reflect God's care for those in our community?
Are there areas in which we treat the goodness of God as an abstract fact rather than a concrete motive of praise?
study.practice: Set up a daily moment to praise God not only for his greatness, but also for his attention to the small and wounded. Remember a situation in which you have been sustained by God in weakness and turn it into prayer of gratitude. Also, look for a concrete way to honor someone who is in a condition of need, shame or invisibility, imitating the God who raises the poor and gives family to the barren.
study.uncertainty: The notes suggest, but do not prove definitively, that the psalm may have been composed after exile and linked to the liturgical use of Easter. There are also distinct interpretations of the application of verses such as 7 and 9: some read above all as general care for the poor and sterile; others, as a possible historical reference to exiles and return. These readings should be treated as interpretations, not as absolute certainty of the text.
